title: Generative Inverse Design of Metamaterials with Functional Responses by Interpretable Learning
summary: Proposes RIGID, a single-shot inverse design method for metamaterials whose design target is a qualitative functional response such as a spectral curve shape, rather than a scalar property value. A random forest is trained as a forward predictor and then inverted, its decision paths read as a likelihood over the design space so that candidate designs are sampled directly without training a deep generative model, which the authors argue also makes the procedure interpretable and cheap on small data. The only Synthetic Data Vault reference is Xu and Veeramachaneni's TGAN, which appears once inside a three-work group citation supporting the claim that generative inverse design handles mixed continuous and categorical design variables poorly without special treatment; no SDV code is run and CTGAN is never named.
evidence: the paper states that the problem involves inverse design with both continuous and categorical variables, which common optimization and generative modeling-based inverse design cannot handle well without special treatment [86, 87, 88], and that its random forest-based method addresses mixed-variable problems without any issues; reference 88 is Lei Xu and Kalyan Veeramachaneni, Synthesizing tabular data using generative adversarial networks, arXiv preprint arXiv:1811.11264, 2018, that is TGAN and not CTGAN; the tight SDV-family pattern matches three times in the whole document, all in or around that one citation; full text read from the arXiv version 2401.00003v6, the Wiley PDF being behind a Cloudflare challenge

title: Privacy Re-Identification Attacks on Tabular GANs
summary: Studies whether tabular GANs leak the records they were trained on, defining three levels of re-identification attack of increasing attacker knowledge and measuring, for each, how many unique training samples are recovered and how close the recovered synthetic records sit to real ones under distance to closest record. Attacks are run against three tabular GANs on the Adult, Lending Club, PAKDD and Taiwan credit datasets, and differential privacy is then tested as a defence against the strongest attack. CTGAN is one of the three generators actually trained and attacked, described by the paper as a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty whose conditional vectors ensure underrepresented discrete categories are modelled, and it is the single model carried into the second research question because it is the cheapest of the three to train.
evidence: the paper states that it selects three state-of-the-art tabular GAN models for generating synthetic data samples of the datasets, and describes CTGAN (Xu et al., 2019) as a Wasserstein-based gradient penalty loss GAN that utilises the selection of conditional vectors during training in order to ensure sufficient modelling of underrepresented discrete categories; the results tables report unique samples attacked and distance to closest record in separate columns for CTGAN, CTAB-GAN and CasTGAN across all three attack levels; the paper further states that it explores RQ2 using CTGAN since it is the most efficient GAN model to train and because the results show no major disparity between the GAN models; full text read from the arXiv version 2404.00696v1, the Wiley PDF being behind a Cloudflare challenge

title: A Framework for Generating Realistic Synthetic Tabular Data in a Randomized Controlled Trial Setting
summary: Sets out a framework for generating synthetic trial data that respects the structure of a randomized controlled trial, distinguishing a simultaneous approach in which one fitted model generates all variables at once from a sequential approach that follows the trial's own order, baseline collection, then randomization, then post-randomization measurements and the final outcome, with lighter regression execution models used for the later steps. The frameworks are evaluated on the ACTG 175 HIV trial and compared against adversarial random forests and an R-vine copula. CTGAN is the generator in both the simultaneous and the sequential framework, selected because the authors judge it the preferred method for mixed-type tabular data and because, as they note, its implementation is well documented through the Synthetic Data Vault library in Python; TVAE was considered and set aside over its handling of minority classes in discrete variables.
evidence: the paper states that CTGANs are the preferred state-of-the-art method for generating tabular data with mixed data types and that their implementation is well-documented through the Synthetic Data Vault library in Python, citing Patki et al., and that it pursues this approach in its investigations; the experimental setup compares the frameworks it terms CTGAN Simultaneous versus CTGAN Sequential alongside ARF Sequential and R-Vine Copula Sequential; the sequential description states that a CTGAN was trained on the real baseline data and the fitted CTGAN used to generate the baseline variables, with execution models fit to each subsequent variable; the paper also states that it did not consider TVAE as it has been shown to perform poorly when a minority class of a discrete variable is present; full text read from the PubMed Central copy PMC12345405

title: Towards Synthesizing High-Dimensional Tabular Data with Limited Samples
summary: Observes that diffusion-based tabular synthesizers degrade as dimensionality grows while the sample count stays fixed, argues that the effective number of samples per dimension is the binding constraint, and proposes CtrTab, which injects controlled noise into the input and adds an L2 regularizer whose form is derived from that noise, so the model is discouraged from memorizing sparse high-dimensional training points. Evaluated on high-dimensional datasets against SMOTE, TabDDPM, RelDDPM and TabSyn under downstream AUC, F1, RMSE and R2. CTGAN and TVAE are two of the six baselines trained and reported in every results table, and the related-work section credits CTGAN with conditioning the generator on class labels and traces that lineage forward to CTAB-GAN+; CtrTab is diffusion-based and does not itself build on CTGAN's conditional vector.
evidence: the paper states that it compares CtrTab with six baseline models including SMOTE, TVAE (Xu et al. 2019), CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019), TabDDPM, RelDDPM and TabSyn; CTGAN and TVAE each occupy their own row in the AUC/RMSE and F1/R2 results tables and in the dimensionality figure; the conditional tabular data synthesis subsection states that CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) incorporates class labels in the generator to produce data conditioned on the target class and that CTAB-GAN+ extends CTGAN to support both discrete and continuous data class labels; no part of CtrTab's own construction reuses that conditional vector; full text read from the arXiv version 2503.06444v2, the AAAI proceedings host returning an upstream error

title: Adaptive differentiable trees for transparent learning on data streams
summary: Introduces soft Hoeffding trees, a differentiable tree model for data streams meant to keep the interpretability of a decision tree while adapting to concept drift through learned routing weights rather than through unbounded depth growth, and evaluates them against streaming tree baselines on stationary and drifting streams. CTGAN supplies the synthetic evaluation data: a CTGAN is fitted to real datasets drawn from the PMLB repository to emulate a realistic distribution over a stream of 10^6 samples, ten abrupt drifts are then induced by oversampling a randomly selected class, and a larger stationary stream of 10^7 instances is generated by the same procedure for the scalability experiments. The generator is infrastructure here; the paper's subject is the tree model.
evidence: the paper states that its streams are derived from real-world data streams from the PMLB repository and that it employs a Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network (CTGAN) (Xu et al., 2019) to emulate a realistic distribution within a substantial data stream of 10^6 samples, with abrupt drifts injected by oversampling a randomly selected class and ten drifts induced; the scalability section states that data streams containing 10^7 instances were generated using the same procedure with CTGAN, without introducing any drifts; the bibliography carries Xu, Skoularidou, Cuesta-Infante and Veeramachaneni, Modeling tabular data using conditional GAN; full text read from the Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz open science repository copy

title: Generating survey databases with Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks
summary: Develops Wasserstein GAN variants for generating official survey databases, taking as the central problem that survey records carry sampling weights which ordinary generators ignore, and incorporating those weights into training under both clipping and gradient-penalty constraints. Tested on the 2019 Belgian Labour Force Survey with 146 variables and scored on Wasserstein distance, FID, SVDD, Cramer-von Mises and KL divergence. CTGAN and CopulaGAN are the two comparison generators, and both are run from the SDV package in Python rather than reimplemented: the paper points to the DataCebo GitHub of the Synthetic Data Vault Project as the source of the code, keeps the default parameters for both, and observes that neither incorporates sampling weights, which is the gap its own methods are built to close.
evidence: the paper states that CopulaGAN first transforms the data before applying CTGAN, that CTGANs use Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty, Gumbel softmax functions, a conditional approach and Gaussian mixture models, and that the code of both CTGAN and CopulaGAN can be found on the DataCebo Github of the Synthetic Data Vault Project; the experimental section states that the authors autonomously developed GANs using Keras and Tensorflow except for two variants based on conditional tabular GANs, CTGAN and CopulaGAN, for which they utilize the implementation provided by the SDV package in Python, and that for the CTGAN and the CopulaGAN within the SDV package they have kept the default parameters, which are the values used in Xu et al.; the paper also states that CopulaGANs and CTGANs do not incorporate sampling weights; full text read from the ORBi Liege repository copy

title: A Combinatorial Approach to Synthetic Data Generation for Machine Learning
summary: Proposes ComGen, which brings combinatorial t-way coverage from software testing to synthetic tabular data generation: attribute values are partitioned into blocks and samples are drawn so that every combination of t attribute values is covered, with t swept from two to five and a differentially private variant also evaluated. Tested on four datasets for downstream model accuracy and F1, statistical similarity and privacy cost. Two of the compared generators, TVAE and CopulaGAN, are taken directly from the SDV framework without any alterations, and SDV supplies the measurement side of the paper as well: the KL divergence and Kolmogorov-Smirnov similarity scores are computed with SDV metrics, as are the NumericalMLP and CategoricalKNN metrics used to score inference-attack privacy cost.
evidence: the paper states that it evaluated its approach against Tabular Variational Autoencoder (TVAE) and CopulaGAN and that it adopted these approaches directly from the SDV framework without any alterations; the evaluation metrics section states that both KLD and KS scores were calculated using SDV metrics, and the privacy cost section states that SDV metrics are used to assess the risk of inference attacks, with the NumericalMLP metric for continuous values and the CategoricalKNN metric for categorical values; the related work section names CTGAN alongside TVAE and CopulaGAN as GAN-based techniques for synthetic tabular data; running SDV's own measurement tooling and not only its synthesizers places this above a pure comparison role, following the DP-CGANS and TRGAN precedent; full text read from the PubMed Central copy PMC12779700

title: PPMI-Benchmark: A Dual Evaluation Framework for Imputation and Synthetic Data Generation in Longitudinal Parkinson's Disease Research
summary: Presents PPMI-Benchmark, a paired evaluation framework for the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative cohort covering longitudinal imputation and synthetic data generation together, comparing six imputation methods and six generators under sliced Wasserstein distance alongside site-level bias measures intended to expose multi-center effects. CTGAN carries the generation half of the benchmark and is the strongest performer on statistical fidelity, and the authors do not run it as shipped: an additional clinical-range term built from indicator functions over the MoCA and UPDRS-III score ranges is added to CTGAN's loss so that generated values stay physiologically plausible, layered on top of the mode-specific normalization and conditional generation the paper credits to Xu et al.
evidence: the paper states that its synthetic data generation framework implemented six methods with particular emphasis on CTGANs, that the CTGAN architecture incorporates mode-specific normalization and conditional generation, and that the authors enhanced the standard implementation with clinical range constraints through indicator functions in the loss term, giving L_clinical as a sum of indicator functions over MCATOT in [0,30] and NP3TOT in [0,108]; the results state that CTGAN demonstrated superior performance in generating synthetic data that preserved the statistical properties of the original PPMI dataset; CTGAN also appears in the keyword list; full text read from the SciTePress PDF at Papers/2025/136497/136497.pdf
